name: Dohány Street Synagogue
description: The Dohány Street Synagogue, built in 1854–1859 in Moorish Revival style, is the largest synagogue in Europe. It is the centre of Budapest's Jewish quarter, with a museum, memorial park and Heroes' Temple, so a visit covers both architecture and history.

children.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue was built between 1854 and 1859 and consecrated on 6 September 1859. Ludwig Förster designed the exterior in the Moorish Revival and Romantic Historicist style, and Frigyes Feszl was responsible for part of the interior design. The twin towers, striped brickwork and rose window make it one of the most distinctive buildings in the city centre.

It is described as the largest synagogue in Europe, seating about 3,000 people, with separate seating for men and in the women's galleries. The original organ, built in 1859, was played by Franz Liszt and Camille Saint-Saëns; the current mechanical organ was built in 1996.

The synagogue stands at the edge of the area that became the Budapest Ghetto in 1944, and it sheltered many people during that winter. More than two thousand people who died in the winter of 1944–45 are buried in its courtyard. The Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park at the rear holds the Holocaust Tree of Life memorial (the Memorial of the Hungarian Jewish Martyrs) by the sculptor Imre Varga.

The complex also includes the Heroes' Temple, added in 1931 and designed by László Vágó and Ferenc Faragó to commemorate Hungarian Jews who died in World War I, and the Jewish Museum, attached in 1931 and standing on the plot where Theodor Herzl's house once stood.

A visit combines a place of worship with a memorial. Check the current visiting rules before you go, since the complex is closed to visitors every Saturday and, according to visitor guides, on Jewish holidays, and the community asks visitors to cover their shoulders and knees, men to cover their heads, and everyone to pass a security check at the entrance.
Good to know
Check the current opening times, ticket options and visiting rules on the official source before you go.
The streets around the synagogue formed the edge of the Budapest Ghetto in 1944; the Jewish Museum and the memorial park are part of the same complex.
Heroes' Temple, the Jewish Museum and the Wallenberg Memorial Park can be visited as part of the same site: ask what your ticket includes.

historySections.heading: A landmark of the nineteenth-century Jewish community

children.text: The synagogue was constructed in the nineteenth century as Budapest's Jewish population expanded. Its distinctive Moorish Revival architecture and monumental scale distinguish it from the city's many churches.
The synagogue and surrounding memorial spaces now connect worship, historic preservation and remembrance of Jewish life and the Holocaust.

name: House of Music Hungary
description: A City Park building by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto, topped by a roof perforated with 100 openings. Exhibitions on the history of music, a sound dome, a concert hall and an open-air stage are spread across three levels in the Liget Budapest museum quarter, with a separate calendar of events.

children.text: The House of Music Hungary, in Hungarian the Magyar Zene Háza, stands in Budapest's City Park and was designed by the Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto. It is part of the government-funded Liget Budapest project, which aims to create a museum quarter in the city's oldest public park. Fujimoto was one of three winners selected in the Liget Budapest museum competition. The house opened to the public in January 2022, with Apollo Magazine giving 23 January as the date, after almost six years of construction according to Archinect.

The building is topped by a large white roof canopy perforated with 100 openings, which channels light deep into an open floor plan. Panels of glass blur the boundary between the interior and the park, and plant life rises from the core of the building. Fujimoto said his team was enchanted by the multitude of trees in City Park. The programme is spread across three levels, and Archinect puts the building at about 97,000 square feet.

According to Archinect, the subterranean level holds permanent and temporary exhibitions as well as a sound dome that creates a hologram-like aural environment, inspired by a concept from the composer Karlheinz Stockhausen. The House's own site describes the Sound Dome, Hangdóm in Hungarian, as an immersive 360-degree cinema room with a dome screen and a surround-sound system. Apollo Magazine describes a gallery of about 1,000 square metres, a permanent exhibition on the history of music in Europe and an inaugural temporary exhibition on Hungarian pop music from 1957 to 1993. The ground level has a concert hall and an open-air stage for performances.

The top level is devoted to educational spaces that present Hungary's musical heritage and draw on the ideas of Klára Kokas and Zoltán Kodály. Archinect names András Batta as managing director and says museum projects by Napur and SANAA were due to follow within the Liget Budapest development. Because exhibitions and concerts change, the official site is the place to see what is currently on.
Good to know
Check the official House of Music site for current exhibitions, concerts and tickets, as the programme includes temporary exhibitions and performances.
The building sits within City Park, so it combines easily with a walk through the park.
The open-air stage is on the ground level, so some performances may depend on the weather; confirm on the event page.

historyIntro: The House of Music brings a new architectural chapter to City Park, connecting Hungary's musical heritage with contemporary design.

children.text: Opened in January 2022 as part of the Liget Budapest project, the House of Music was designed by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto. Its unusual roof, glass walls and relationship to the surrounding trees make the building itself a reason to visit.

The institution combines the history of music with exhibitions, education and live events. Its themes reach beyond classical composers to sound technology and popular music, placing Hungarian traditions in an international story.

name: Margaret Island
description: Margaret Island is a 2.5-kilometre park in the middle of the Danube, largely closed to cars, with gardens, a music fountain, a Japanese garden, a water tower, pools and a running track. It lies between Buda and Pest and is reached from Margaret Bridge.

children.text: Margaret Island lies in the Danube in central Budapest, between Margaret Bridge to the south and Árpád Bridge to the north. It is about 2.5 kilometres long and 500 metres wide, with an area of around 0.965 square kilometres. In its present form it was created at the end of the 19th century by joining three smaller islands, the Festő, Fürdő and Nyulak islands, to control the river's flow.

Before the 14th century it was known as the Island of Rabbits. Its modern name comes from Saint Margaret (1242–1270), the daughter of King Béla IV, who lived in the Dominican convent on the island. Religious houses dominated the island until the 16th century; during the Ottoman wars the monks and nuns fled and the buildings were destroyed. It became a resort of the palatines in the 18th century and was declared a public garden in 1908.

Today it is a public park in the middle of the city. Motor traffic is restricted: you cannot drive through the island, driving in needs an entry permit, and bus line 26 runs through it, so you can walk, run or cycle in relative peace. A rubber-coated running track is about 5.35 kilometres long. You can rent four-person pedal carts and small electric cars.

Among the sights are the Music Fountain and the Music Well, the Japanese Garden, a small zoo, the Centennial Memorial of 1973 by István Kiss, and the octagonal Art Nouveau water tower of 1911. The island also has large sports and bathing facilities, including the Palatinus open-air swimming complex and the Alfréd Hajós sports pool, and an open-air theatre.
Good to know

The island lies between Margaret Bridge and Árpád Bridge; you cannot drive through the island and entering by car needs a permit, so plan to arrive on foot or by public transport; the only parking is a paid car park at the northern end, and the access rules are best checked before you travel.
Pedal carts and small electric cars can be rented on the island if you do not want to walk its whole length.
Bring a swimsuit if you plan to use the Palatinus open-air complex: check the current opening dates.

children.text: The island occupies a wide stretch of the Danube between Buda and Pest. Medieval religious communities once lived here, and the ruins of their buildings remain among the island's walking routes.
Its parks, pathways and leisure attractions now provide a quieter contrast to the surrounding city.

name: St. Stephen's Hall
description: A reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace, designed by Alajos Hauszmann around 1900 and gutted in the Second World War. Rebuilt over decades from photographs and plans, with a large Zsolnay ceramic fireplace, it opened to visitors in 2021.

children.text: St. Stephen's Hall, Szent István-terem, is a reconstructed ceremonial interior in the Buda Castle palace. It is named after Saint Stephen, founder of the Hungarian state, and was one of the most important interiors of the palace during the Dual Monarchy. Budapest.com says it was part of the palace's expansion after the Compromise of 1867, with architect Alajos Hauszmann designing it as the showpiece of the state rooms.

According to We Love Budapest, the original room had a carved ceiling, a large ceramic fireplace with Zsolnay depictions of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints, gilded furnishings and large chandeliers. Vilmos Zsolnay made the ceramics, Endre Thék the carved furniture and interior, and the Neuschloss brothers the parquet inlay. Budapest.com gives the fireplace as about 4.5 metres high and 2.5 metres wide, made of more than 600 pieces, with a bust of Saint Stephen by Alajos Stróbl on the mantelpiece. The interior was shown at the 1900 Paris World's Fair, where it won a top prize, before being installed in the palace. Emperor Franz Joseph called it very beautiful on his visit.

The hall hosted royal audiences and working lunches and served as a card room during balls. In December 1916, the day before the coronation of Karl I, the chest holding the Holy Crown was opened in the hall before the crown was taken to Matthias Church; this was the last ceremonial use of the room.

The Second World War ended the hall's life. The palace was bombed and fire gutted the interior, and the southern connecting wing suffered the most damage in the siege of 1944 and 1945. The room then stood unrestored and was used as storage for decades. Reconstruction began only in the post-communist era and took a long time, using archive photographs, plans, old invoices, duplicate ceiling pieces from the Zsolnay Quarter in Pécs and a transcript found in a villa on Lendvay utca. It was carried out under the National Hauszmann Program.

The reconstructed hall opened to the public in 2021, and We Love Budapest says visits are by guided tour. The accompanying exhibition, The Miracle of Buda Castle, includes a ten-door installation by Sam Havadtoy based on The Admonitions, a Latin text attributed to a foreign cleric and dated to around the 1010s. The hall also displays a very large herm, a sculpted likeness of Saint Stephen.
Good to know
Visits are by guided tour, according to a 2021 report; check the official St. Stephen's Hall site for current tours, languages and tickets.
Look first at the Zsolnay ceramic fireplace and the portraits of Árpád-dynasty kings and saints around the walls.
The hall is in the Buda Castle palace area, where the Matthias Fountain and the Savoyai Terrace also lie.

historyIntro: St Stephen's Hall recalls the decorative splendour of the royal palace and the losses that transformed Castle Hill in the twentieth century.

historySections.heading: A royal interior from the turn of the century

children.text: The room originally belonged to the expanded Royal Palace complex and was designed to celebrate Hungarian craftsmanship and the legacy of the country's first king. Rich timber decoration, ceramics and historical ornament gave the room a ceremonial character.

The palace suffered severe wartime damage, and the original hall was lost. The reconstructed room is presented to visitors as part of the Castle Museum's palace heritage, with a separate exhibition and ticketing arrangement from other museum spaces.
